extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning proofs and basic set/function theory (introductory discrete math/analysis)
extracted.subtask_description: Proving and reasoning about functions (one-to-one, onto, inverses), images/inverse-images of sets, and using mathematical induction; includes proof techniques and common pitfalls. Geared to writing rigorous textbook-style proofs and constructing counterexamples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverse of a bijection is a function
rubrics_metrics.description: If f : A -> B is one-to-one and onto, then f^{-1} : B -> A (Theorem 5.3.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof form: let b be arbitrary in B and prove existence and uniqueness separately. Existence uses that f is onto (there is some a with f(a)=b). Uniqueness uses that f is one-to-one (if two a's map to same b they must be equal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of f^{-1} when it is a function
rubrics_metrics.description: If f^{-1}: B -> A is a function, then for each b in B, f^{-1}(b) is the unique a in A such that f(a)=b.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this viewpoint to compute formulas for inverses: solve f(y)=x for y to get f^{-1}(x). This requires there to be exactly one solution for each x.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two functions are equal iff pointwise equal (use for inverses)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove two functions are equal, show for every element of the domain their values agree (Theorem 5.1.4 style; used in proofs such as f^{-1} o f = id).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical proof: let a be arbitrary element of domain and compute both sides at a, showing equality. This pointwise method is recommended and used repeatedly (see commentary after Theorem 5.3.2).

rubrics_metrics.name: If inverse exists then compositions are identities
rubrics_metrics.description: If f:A->B and f^{-1}:B->A is a function then f^{-1} o f = id_A and f o f^{-1} = id_B (Theorem 5.3.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof technique: let a be arbitrary in A, set b=f(a), note (b,a) in f^{-1}, so f^{-1}(b)=a, hence (f^{-1} o f)(a)=a. Similar reasoning for the other composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Left/right inverses imply injectivity/surjectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: If there exists g:B->A with g o f = id_A then f is one-to-one; if there exists g with f o g = id_B then f is onto (Theorem 5.3.3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof idea: apply g to equal values f(a1)=f(a2) to deduce a1=a2. For surjectivity, show every b in B has a preimage via g(b). Note: assumptions are existential (there exists g), so in proofs choose such a g.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence circle for bijectivity and inverses
rubrics_metrics.description: The following are equivalent for f:A->B: (1) f is one-to-one and onto; (2) f^{-1}:B->A is a function; (3) there exists g:B->A with g o f = id_A and f o g = id_B (Theorem 5.3.4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove a cycle of implications (1->2->3->1). Use previous theorems to justify each implication. The text recommends the circle-of-implications proof pattern for equivalence statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness of inverse when both left and right inverses exist
rubrics_metrics.description: If f:A->B and g:B->A satisfy g o f = id_A and f o g = id_B then g = f^{-1} (Theorem 5.3.5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof can use composition manipulations and prior theorems for a short argument; an alternative direct proof checks membership of pairs (b,a) in both relations to show equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to find an inverse formula
rubrics_metrics.description: To find f^{-1}(x) (when it exists) solve the equation f(y)=x for y and express y in terms of x (used in examples such as linear/affine maps and rational examples).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After finding a candidate g, check both g o f = id_A and f o g = id_B. Example: solving 1/y + 2 = x to get g(x)=1/(x-2) and then verifying compositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pitfall: checking both compositions
rubrics_metrics.description: It is possible for one composition to be the identity while the other is not (so a candidate 'inverse' fails). Example: squaring and principal square root — f(x)=x^2, g(x)=√x has f o g = id_B but g o f ≠ id_A, so g is not f^{-1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always verify both g o f = id_A and f o g = id_B to confirm g is the inverse. Use counterexamples to show why uniqueness/existence conditions fail when f not one-to-one or not onto.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of image and inverse image of sets
rubrics_metrics.description: For f:A->B and X⊆A, f(X) = { f(x) | x∈X }. For Y⊆B, f^{-1}(Y) = { a∈A | f(a) ∈ Y } (Definition 5.4.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inverse image f^{-1}(Y) is defined as a set for any f, whether or not f is invertible as a function. Do not assume f^{-1}(y) is meaningful pointwise unless f is a bijection. Examples: cities->countries mapping and inverse images of regions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Image of intersection inclusion and equality condition
rubrics_metrics.description: For f:A->B and W,X⊆A, f(W ∩ X) ⊆ f(W) ∩ f(X). Furthermore, if f is one-to-one then f(W ∩ X) = f(W) ∩ f(X) (Theorem 5.4.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by taking an arbitrary element of f(W ∩ X) and showing it lies in both f(W) and f(X). For the reverse inclusion injectivity is needed; provide counterexamples when f not one-to-one (e.g., f={ (1,4),(2,5),(3,5) } with W={2}, X={3}).

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for proving equality of two sets
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove S = T, prove S ⊆ T and T ⊆ S by taking an arbitrary element of each and showing membership in the other (used repeatedly in the text).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common structure: start with 'let y be arbitrary element of S' and deduce y∈T; then repeat with roles reversed. When equality fails, construct counterexamples focusing on failure points in the inclusion proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy for constructing counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: When a general equality/inclusion seems false, look for functions violating required hypotheses (e.g., not one-to-one) and choose subsets that include witnesses to that failure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From a broken proof, identify where a step required additional property (like injectivity). Then pick f lacking that property and pick sets W, X containing elements demonstrating the failure (the text gives explicit small finite examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolving notation ambiguity for inverse images vs inverse function images
rubrics_metrics.description: If f:A->B is a bijection, then the inverse image of Y⊆B under f (denoted f^{-1}(Y)) equals the image of Y under the function f^{-1}:B->A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To show equality, write out definitions of the two sets and verify element membership equivalence. The text notes this ambiguity is harmless when f is bijective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by mathematical induction (basic scheme)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove ∀n∈N P(n): (1) prove base case P(0) (or appropriate starting n), and (2) prove the induction step ∀n∈N (P(n) ⇒ P(n+1)). Then conclude ∀n P(n) (Section 6.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form of final proof: Base case followed by Induction step. In the induction step, let n be arbitrary, assume P(n) (the inductive hypothesis), and deduce P(n+1). The base case may start at some other integer (e.g., n=5) if the theorem's domain requires it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using inductive hypothesis when it provides an existential witness
rubrics_metrics.description: When the inductive hypothesis asserts an existence (∃k such that ...), instantiate that witness and use it to construct a witness for the next case (Example 6.1.2 where 3 | (n^2 − n)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard tactic: from '3k = n^2 − n' pick k and then algebraically build j = k + n^2 + n (or similar) to show 3 divides (n+1)^2 − (n+1). Do not omit exhibiting the new witness.
